obernants.approximation_semantics: Source-derived exact target relation; finite evidence is not a general proof.
obernants.assumptions: Successful allocation; exact bytes and stated transformation premises.
obernants.domain: Finite byte slices and ordinary terminating Rust calls with successful allocation.
obernants.operator: Within U of finite (text,pattern,bool) observations, exclude true when no whole-string token consumption exists and false when one exists. Anchoring forbids an interior literal match by itself. Bytes outside '?' and '*' remain literal, including backslash; Unicode scalar or path-separator semantics are absent.

obernants.operator: For fixed pattern P and result true, the fiber is exactly its byte language L(P); for false it is the complement within finite byte strings. Many distinct texts match '*'. A Boolean and pattern cannot recover a unique original text or its allocation history.

obernants.operator: At text prefix length i, row[j] equals membership of T[..i] in P[..j]. Fixing a row retains all text prefixes with the same vector of prefix memberships; in-place diagonal/above temporaries preserve the previous row observations until used.

obernants.operator: Replacing any nonempty run of consecutive stars by one star preserves the recognized full-string language, since all nonnegative compositions of consumed lengths have the same possible total. This law does not replace or remove question marks.

obernants.operator: If P has q nonstar tokens, every accepted text has length at least q; with no stars length must equal q. A pattern of q question marks accepts exactly length q. All stars accept every finite text, including empty.

obernants.operator: For a pattern containing neither '?' nor '*', L(P) is the singleton {P}. On this restricted pattern domain, a successful match fixes the input bytes; adding a wildcard generally restores ambiguity.

obernants.operator: Under byte semantics a two-byte UTF-8 character needs two question marks; a scalar-aware counterfactual would require one. Backslash is literal even immediately before '*', so backslash-star accepts a literal backslash followed by any bytes, not a lone literal star.

obernants.operator: For star at pattern position j, accepting (i,j+1) is equivalent to accepting (i,j) with zero new bytes OR (i-1,j+1) with one more byte, for i>0. Replacing OR by AND loses witnesses such as nonempty text matched by one star.
